text: This isn't about automating incident response in general. It's one specific, well-understood step inside almost every account-compromise incident: once a user's account is confirmed compromised, disable sign-in and kill any session the attacker is already holding.

The SOC Operations course's SOAR chapters drew a clear line: automate the well-understood, repeatable portion of a workload, and leave novel judgment calls and high-stakes irreversible actions to a human. Disabling a compromised account and revoking its sessions sits squarely on the automatable side — it's reversible, the correct action never changes case to case, and delay has a real cost, since every minute an attacker keeps an active session is a minute they can keep acting as that user. Deciding the account is actually compromised, and whether anything more drastic is warranted, stays a human's job.

The script uses the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK, the modern way to manage Entra ID accounts, and takes one input: the compromised user's UPN. Connect-MgGraph authenticates with exactly the two scopes this script needs, and Get-MgUser resolves that UPN to the user object the next two cmdlets act on.

Update-MgUser -AccountEnabled:$false stops the account from signing in again. Revoke-MgUserSignInSession invalidates the refresh tokens behind any session it currently holds — without that second call, a session the attacker opened before the account was disabled could keep working until its access token naturally expires. Running both together closes that gap completely.

The Mandatory parameter means this script never runs without an explicit, deliberately chosen target — no default user, no guessing who looks suspicious. A human decides who, and the script's only job is executing those two actions correctly and instantly once that decision is already made. It never decides compromise, investigates, notifies anyone, or re-enables the account — each of those stays a separate, deliberate step.

That's the chapter: cost, compliance, backups, and now a bounded security action, all automated the same way. Next up, Chapter 7: why automation scripts belong in source control — every script this chapter built needs a home besides someone's laptop.
